title: Teachers of the year
hookLine: Job, Patacara, Julian, Frankl, Rabia, Kabir, Thérèse, Corrie ten Boom

lines: THE ASHES. A ROAD. A SICKBED. A CAMP.
cards: Who would you hire to teach a class on hard things? Not a man in the ashes, scraping himself with broken pottery. Or a young mother wandering a road with nothing left.
Or a woman so ill the people at her bed think she's dying. Or a prisoner in a camp, holding on to one reason to get through the night. A strange faculty.
Yet when this year's questions got hard, these were the people who did the teaching: eight of them.

teach.h: JOB AND PATACARA: GRIEF, OUT LOUD.
teach.b: First, the ones who grieved out loud. Job loses his children, his wealth and his health, and won't accept his friends' tidy explanations.
At the end, God tells those friends: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The one who argued spoke rightly.
Patacara, as the Buddhist commentary tells it, loses her family and wanders out of her mind with grief. She meets the Buddha, comes back to herself, becomes a nun, and in time a teacher of others.

teach.h: JULIAN AND FRANKL: HOLDING ON INSIDE IT.
teach.b: Second, the ones who held on inside the pain. Julian of Norwich, in her showings, wondered why sin had not been prevented, and heard: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well."
Viktor Frankl, writing after the camps, argued that one freedom can't be taken from a person: the freedom to choose an attitude. Neither pretended the pain was small.

Third, the ones who loved and forgave without bargaining. In a story people tell, Rabia of Basra walks with a torch and a bucket of water, to burn paradise and put out hell, so that God is loved for God alone.
Kabir, in a verse kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that where there is forgiveness, there is God.

teach.h: THÉRÈSE AND CORRIE: SMALL, AND HARD.
teach.b: Fourth, the ones who made it small and kept it hard. Thérèse of Lisieux called hers a little way: no great deeds, just the smallest things, done out of love.
Corrie ten Boom, whose sister died in Ravensbrück, writes in The Hiding Place of a former guard holding out his hand, and of taking it.
Eight teachers from many paths, each still exactly who they are, none asked to agree with the others.

how: People on many paths keep their teachers close by retelling their stories, reading their words, and remembering them by name; some write letters to teachers they never met as a way of saying what they learned.

o: a Pali word for the calm that comes after grief
the Buddha's mother, who died soon after his birth
a grieving mother who became a Buddhist nun and teacher

p: argued, and God said he spoke rightly
a torch and a bucket of water

s: at the end of the book of Job, God sides with the friends who explained his suffering
God tells the friends they have not spoken rightly, as Job has (Job 42:7).
Rabia's torch and bucket comes from a verse of the Quran
it's a story people tell about her, not scripture.
Thérèse of Lisieux called her way a little way: the smallest things, done out of love
no great deeds; she made holiness small enough to fit an ordinary day.

games.q: you're one of Job's friends. he has lost everything, and he's angry at heaven. what do you do?
o: explain that his suffering must be punishment for something.
tell him to stop arguing with God.
stay with him, and let his complaint stand.
games.why: the friends explained, and at the end of the book God says they had not spoken rightly, while Job, who argued, had.

practice: Pick one of the eight, or another teacher from this year, or someone in your life who taught you the same thing. Write them one line, as inside a card: what you took from them, or what you're still learning.
If you pray, you can hold that teacher in prayer; if not, let the line rest while you sit.
